usage: Polite-neutral; the first thing you ask someone who's hurt or upset
반말, to a friend or someone younger/close
Honorific 으세요, to an elder, a customer, or a stranger
Follow-up when they may be physically injured
examples: 괜찮아요?
Are you okay?
Said the instant you see someone stumble, cry, or look pale
많이 놀랐죠? 괜찮아요?
That must have been a shock — are you okay?
놀랐죠 acknowledges the fright before checking on them
얼굴이 안 좋아 보여요. 무슨 일 있어요? 괜찮으세요?
You don't look well. Is something wrong? Are you all right?

nuance: 괜찮아요? is the all-purpose 'are you okay?' and it is the single most useful comfort line a newcomer can have — it works for someone who tripped, who got bad news, who looks sad, or who just had a fright. The verb 괜찮다 means 'to be fine / all right / acceptable', so as a question it checks on the person's state. Register matters a lot here: to a friend you say 괜찮아?, to an elder, a stranger, or a customer you must lift it to 괜찮으세요? with the honorific -으세요, and the flat 괜찮아요? sits politely in the middle. The near-miss learners make is confusing it with 괜찮아요 as a STATEMENT — the very same words said with falling intonation mean 'I'm fine / it's okay / no thank you', so tone (rising = question, falling = reassurance) does all the work. The classic English-speaker pitfall is over-translating 'Are you okay?' into something like 당신 괜찮습니까 — dropping 당신 ('you'), which sounds cold and textbook-ish in Korean; you almost never say 당신 to someone's face. Just say 괜찮아요? and let context supply the 'you'. Don't pair it with 너 to a stranger either; that's 반말 and rude.

usage: Hang in there / You got this
반말; to a close friend or someone younger
Polite; to a peer or someone you're not super close with
Honorific; to an elder, a coworker, or a customer
Stay strong, it'll all work out
Pairing it with reassurance about the future
examples: 힘내!
Hang in there!
Said to a friend before an exam, interview, or tough day
요즘 많이 힘들지? 힘내.
Things are rough lately, huh? Hang in there.
힘들지 acknowledges the struggle before the encouragement
많이 지치셨죠. 그래도 힘내세요. 제가 응원할게요.
You must be worn out. Still, please hang in there — I'm rooting for you.
응원할게요 ('I'll cheer you on') makes the support concrete
nuance: 힘내 is 힘 ('strength/energy') + 내다 ('to put out/summon'), literally 'put out your strength' — the everyday way to tell someone to keep going, stay strong, or cheer up when they're tired, stressed, or facing something hard. It is encouragement aimed at the FUTURE effort, not sympathy for what already happened, so you say it before an exam, during a rough patch, or to someone job-hunting. Register climbs cleanly: 힘내 (friend) → 힘내요 (peer) → 힘내세요 (elder/coworker/customer). The crucial contrast is with 힘들어 ('it's hard / I'm struggling', from the adjective 힘들다) — beginners constantly mix up 힘내 ('summon strength', a command to the other person) and 힘들어 ('it's tough', describing a state); they share 힘 but mean opposite things. The big English-speaker pitfall is using 힘내 at a FUNERAL or for a death — there 힘내세요 can sound tone-deaf, almost like 'snap out of it', because the person isn't facing a challenge to push through, they're grieving; for loss you use 삼가 고인의 명복을 빕니다 or 마음이 아프네요 instead. Also avoid the over-literal 'fighting!' substitution: 화이팅 is upbeat pep (sports, go-get-em), while 힘내 carries real warmth for someone hurting.

usage: Polite; reassuring a peer or someone you respect
Add 다 ('all') to widen the reassurance
곧 ('soon') when you want to promise it won't last
examples: 괜찮아질 거예요.
It'll be okay.
Said to someone worried about a problem that will pass
지금은 힘들어도 곧 괜찮아질 거예요.
Even if it's hard now, it'll be okay soon.
Contrast 지금은 힘들어도 ('though hard now') with the hopeful future
시간이 좀 걸리겠지만, 다 괜찮아질 거예요. 너무 걱정 마요.
It may take some time, but everything will be okay. Don't worry too much.
Soften with 걱정 마요 ('don't worry') for extra comfort

The key piece learners drop is the -아지- in the middle: 괜찮다 alone is a STATE ('it is okay'), while 괜찮아지다 is the CHANGE ('it becomes okay'), and you need the change verb to say it'll IMPROVE; saying 괜찮을 거예요 ('it will be okay') is also fine and common, but 괜찮아질 거예요 specifically conveys 'it'll get better from how it is now'. Another trap: don't use this for a death or a truly irreversible loss, where 'it'll be okay' rings hollow; reserve it for situations that genuinely can improve. usage: 반말; to a close friend or someone younger
Polite; to a peer or acquaintance
Honorific; to an elder, customer, or boss
Add 너무 to soften an outright 'don't'
examples: 걱정하지 마.
Don't worry.
Said to reassure a friend stressing over something
내가 도와줄게. 걱정하지 마.
I'll help you, so don't worry.
Pair with 도와줄게 ('I'll help') to back up the comfort
잘 해결될 테니까 너무 걱정하지 마세요. 제가 옆에 있잖아요.
It'll work out, so please don't worry too much. I'm right here with you.
옆에 있잖아요 ('I'm beside you') makes the reassurance personal

usage: Polite-neutral; opening when someone looks upset
Honorific; to an elder, customer, or boss
혹시 ('perhaps') makes the question gentler, less prying
examples: 무슨 일 있어요?
Is something wrong?
Asked when someone seems off, quiet, or upset
표정이 안 좋네요. 무슨 일 있어요?
You look down. Is something wrong?
표정이 안 좋다 ('your expression is bad') invites them to open up
혹시 무슨 일 있으세요? 제가 도울 일 있으면 말씀하세요.
Is something the matter? If there's anything I can do, please tell me.
Offer help with 도울 일 있으면 to show you mean it
nuance: 무슨 일 있어요? is 무슨 ('what kind of') + 일 ('matter/thing/event') + 있어요 ('is there'), literally 'is there some matter?' — the natural opener when you notice someone looks troubled and you want to gently ask what's going on. 일 here is the broad word for 'a happening/issue', not 'work', though it CAN mean work in other contexts — context disambiguates. Register: 있어? (friend) → 있어요? (neutral) → 있으세요? (honorific, where 있다 politely becomes 있으세요). The softener 혹시 ('perhaps, by any chance') is golden for this phrase: 혹시 무슨 일 있어요? feels caring rather than nosy. The contrast to know is 무슨 일이에요? ('what is it? / what's the matter?', asking the nature of a known issue) vs. 무슨 일 있어요? ('is something wrong?', checking whether there IS an issue) — close but the first assumes something's up, the second probes. The English-speaker pitfall is the particle: learners say 무슨 일을 있어요 (object 을) — but 있다 ('to exist') takes the subject marker or none, never 을; it's 무슨 일(이) 있어요. Another trap is translating 'what's wrong WITH you' too literally and sounding accusatory — 무슨 일 있어요? is warm and open, so keep it that way; don't add 너 (you) to a stranger.

english: Oh no, what do we do
usage: Polite; a sympathetic reaction to someone's bad news
반말; to a close friend, often half-gasped
Oh dear, what should we do
Oh, what a thing / good heavens
examples: 어머, 어떡해요.
Oh my, that's awful.
어머 + 어떡해요 is the instinctive reaction to sudden bad news
지갑을 잃어버렸다고요? 어떡해요.
You lost your wallet? Oh no.
Echo their problem, then 어떡해요 to share the dismay
저런, 그렇게 됐다니 정말 어떡해요. 많이 놀라셨겠어요.
Oh dear, to think it turned out that way — what a thing. You must have been so shaken.
Chain with 놀라셨겠어요 to deepen the sympathy
nuance: 어떡해요 is a contraction of 어떻게 해요 ('how do (we/you) do?'), but as a set exclamation it has bleached into 'oh no / what a shame / what'll you do' — a reflexive, warm reaction you blurt out when someone tells you something distressing (a loss, an accident, a piece of bad luck). It signals 'I feel for you, this is awful' rather than literally asking for a plan. Register: 어떡해 (friend) → 어떡해요 (polite); to an elder you'd more likely shift to 이를 어째요 or pair it with sympathy like 많이 놀라셨겠어요. The crucial spelling/meaning split is 어떡해 vs. 어떻게: 어떻게 ('how') is the question word used WITH another verb (어떻게 해요, 어떻게 가요), while 어떡해 is the standalone exclamation/contraction and can NOT take another verb after it — writing 어떡해 가요 is wrong; it's 어떻게 가요. This is one of the most-confused pairs for learners. The English-speaker pitfall is taking 어떡해요 literally as 'how should I do it?' and waiting for instructions, or answering it as a real question — in sympathy it's just 'oh no'. Another trap is overusing it for tiny inconveniences; it carries real concern, so save it for genuinely bad news, not a spilled coffee (there you'd say 아이고 or 어머).

english: You worked hard / Thanks for your effort
usage: You've worked hard / Thanks for the effort
Polite; to a peer or someone junior after hard work
반말; to a close friend or someone younger
Thank you for your hard work
Honorific; to an elder, senior, or someone you respect
You've been through so much / worked so hard
Add 많다 to stress just how much effort it took
examples: 오늘 고생했어요.
You worked hard today.
Said to a coworker at the end of a long day
먼 길 오느라 고생하셨어요. 좀 쉬세요.
Thank you for coming all this way — you must be tired. Please rest.
오느라 ('in the course of coming') ties the effort to a specific act
힘든 일 겪으시느라 고생 많으셨어요. 이제 좀 나아지셨어요?
You've been through so much — are you feeling a bit better now?
겪으시느라 ('in going through it') turns it into sympathy for hardship
nuance: 고생했어요 is 고생 ('hardship/toil', Sino-Korean 苦生) + 하다 in the past, literally 'you went through hardship' — a warm acknowledgment that someone put in real effort or endured something tough. Honorific; to an elder or someone you respect

english: You've got me / I'm here for you

Polite; to a peer or someone you respect a bit

무슨 일 있으면 언제든 말해. 내가 있잖아.

english: I don't know if this is any comfort, but...
usage: I don't know if this helps, but...
Polite-formal; humble lead-in before offering comfort
Not sure this comforts you, but...

I hope my words are some comfort
A warm closing wish after speaking
I hardly know what words of comfort to offer
When you're lost for words at deep grief
examples: 위로가 될지 모르겠지만, 제가 늘 응원하고 있어요.
I don't know if it's any comfort, but I'm always rooting for you.

위로가 될지 모르겠지만, 시간이 약이라고 하잖아요.
I don't know if this helps, but they say time heals, right?
시간이 약 ('time is medicine') is a classic comforting saying
뭐라 위로의 말씀을 드려야 할지 모르겠습니다. 그저 마음이 아플 뿐입니다.
I hardly know what words of comfort to offer. I just feel the pain of it deeply.

This is more advanced, adult register, exactly what you'd say to a grieving coworker, a friend who lost a job, or anyone facing something heavy — it shows emotional tact. The verb 위로하다 ('to console') and noun 위로 ('comfort') are the core vocabulary of this whole situation; 위로가 되다 means 'to BE a comfort / to be comforting'. english: My deepest condolences (may the deceased rest in peace)
usage: May the deceased rest in peace
Slightly shorter, still formal and proper
Very formal, common in written messages/wreaths
I'm at a loss for words
Said in person to the bereaved, paired with the above
examples: 삼가 고인의 명복을 빕니다.
My deepest condolences.
The set phrase, said or written when someone has passed
부친상 소식 들었습니다. 삼가 고인의 명복을 빕니다.
I heard the news of your father's passing. My deepest condolences.
부친상 ('father's funeral') names the loss before the condolence
갑작스러운 비보에 뭐라 드릴 말씀이 없습니다. 삼가 고인의 명복을 빕니다.
At such sudden, sorrowful news I'm at a loss for words. My deepest condolences.
비보 ('tragic news') + 말씀이 없다 sets a solemn, respectful tone
nuance: 삼가 고인의 명복을 빕니다 is the fixed, formal condolence formula: 삼가 ('respectfully, humbly') + 고인 ('the deceased', 故人) + 의 (possessive) + 명복 ('the bliss of the afterlife', 冥福) + 을 + 빕니다 ('I pray', from 빌다), literally 'I respectfully pray for the deceased's peace in the afterlife' — Korea's standard equivalent of 'my deepest condolences / rest in peace'. This is THE thing to say or write at a funeral (장례식), in a condolence text, or on a wreath ribbon. It is high, formal register by nature (it's a ritual phrase), so you keep -ㅂ니다 and do NOT casualize it. Crucially, you say this ABOUT the deceased and to/around the bereaved; the huge English-speaker pitfall is saying comfort meant for the LIVING here — e.g. 힘내세요 ('stay strong') or 괜찮아질 거예요 ('it'll be okay') can sound jarringly light at a wake, so 삼가 고인의 명복을 빕니다 (and to the family, 얼마나 상심이 크세요 'how great your grief must be', or 뭐라 드릴 말씀이 없습니다 'I'm lost for words') is the correct tone. Also note the origin of 명복 is Buddhist, but the phrase is used universally regardless of religion (for a devout Christian family some prefer 삼가 조의를 표합니다 'I offer condolences', which is religion-neutral). structuredNuance.t: 삼가 고인의 명복을 빕니다 literally means 'I respectfully pray for the deceased's peace in the afterlife' — Korea's standard equivalent of 'my deepest condolences / rest in peace'. This is THE thing to say or write at a funeral (장례식), in a condolence text, or on a wreath ribbon. It is high, formal register by nature (it's a ritual phrase), so you keep -ㅂ니다 and do NOT casualize it.

It is the fixed, formal condolence formula: 삼가 ('respectfully, humbly') + 고인 ('the deceased', 故人) + 의 (possessive) + 명복 ('the bliss of the afterlife', 冥福) + 을 + 빕니다 ('I pray', from 빌다). The origin of 명복 is Buddhist, but the phrase is used universally regardless of religion (for a devout Christian family some prefer 삼가 조의를 표합니다 'I offer condolences', which is religion-neutral).

You say this ABOUT the deceased and to/around the bereaved; the huge pitfall is saying comfort meant for the LIVING here — e.g. 힘내세요 ('stay strong') or 괜찮아질 거예요 ('it'll be okay') can sound jarringly light at a wake, so 삼가 고인의 명복을 빕니다 (and to the family, 얼마나 상심이 크세요 'how great your grief must be', or 뭐라 드릴 말씀이 없습니다 'I'm lost for words') is the correct tone. The phrase honors the deceased, so don't misapply it to someone merely sick or struggling — it's specifically for death. Also parse it as one unit; don't drop 삼가.

mistakes: Saying 힘내세요 or 괜찮아질 거예요 at a funeral.
Those are for the living facing a challenge and sound too light at a wake. The proper condolence is 삼가 고인의 명복을 빕니다; to the family, 얼마나 상심이 크세요 or 뭐라 드릴 말씀이 없습니다.
Using it for someone who is merely sick or struggling.
고인 means 'the deceased' and 명복 is afterlife peace — this phrase is ONLY for a death. For someone ill, say 얼른 쾌차하세요 / 몸조리 잘하세요 instead.
Casualizing it (e.g. 고인의 명복을 빌어 / 빌어요).
It's a formal ritual phrase; keep the formal 빕니다. Dropping to 반말 or even 빌어요 sounds wrong at a solemn occasion. Say the full 삼가 고인의 명복을 빕니다.
